customConcept.name: Windows on the World
customConcept.blurb: The 107th floor of the World Trade Center: a tiered dining room facing north and east over Manhattan, a bar with the best view in the city, and the biggest wine list New York has ever seen.

state.circumstances: January 1999. You run Windows on the World, the restaurant complex on the 106th and 107th floors of the North Tower of the World Trade Center, under a lease from the Port Authority. It reopened in June 1996 after a $25 million renovation; this year the Cellar in the Sky room becomes Wild Blue, a 60-seat steakhouse. There are about 450 people on the payroll, Kevin Zraly's wine school, banquet and conference rooms on the 106th floor, and tourists who ride 107 floors to see the view and stay for a drink. Money here is in 1999 dollars.

features.name: The view from the 107th floor
features.pitch: Floor-to-ceiling windows facing north and east over Manhattan, from the Empire State Building to the bridges.

features.name: The Greatest Bar on Earth
features.pitch: A 300-person room of chef stations rolling sushi, shucking oysters and stirring shabu-shabu, loud and a little wild, with Latin bands on Thursday nights.

features.name: Banquet and conference rooms on the 106th floor
features.pitch: Private rooms for weddings, Wall Street dinners, corporate breakfasts and conferences.

features.name: Windows on the World Wine School
features.pitch: Kevin Zraly's evening wine classes, which send students straight to the list.

setting.name: 107th floor, North Tower, World Trade Center
setting.desc: The top of the North Tower in Lower Manhattan, 1999. Brokers and bankers from the Financial District at lunch, tourists from everywhere who come up for the view, weddings and Wall Street dinners in the banquet rooms, and a bar where the city lights stretch to the horizon.

ev.text: Cloud sat on the top of the tower for three days. Diners booked for the view looked out at white.
Wall Street bonus season: every banquet room is booked for holiday parties through New Year's.
A fashion magazine shot its spring issue in the dining room at dawn.

desk.title: New Year's Eve 1999
desk.text: Every party planner in the city wants the room for the millennium. You could sell it as one private event, or keep it open at a very high prix fixe.

world.notes: Windows on the World occupied the 106th and 107th floors of the North Tower of the World Trade Center, about 50,000 square feet, developed by Joe Baum and first opened in 1976. After the February 1993 bombing it closed; the Port Authority chose a new operator in 1994 and it reopened on June 27, 1996 after a $25 million renovation designed by Hugh Hardy, with jackets still required in the main dining room (neckties optional) and the Greatest Bar on Earth in place of the old City Lights Bar and Hors d'Oeuvrerie: a 300-person room of chef stations for sushi, oysters and shabu-shabu, microbrews, vodkas, wines by the glass and about 25 international dishes, with Latin bands on Thursday nights. In 1999 Cellar in the Sky became Wild Blue, a 60-seat American steakhouse. Joe Baum died in 1998. Michael Lomonaco became executive chef in 1997 and replaced the old menus with American cooking from the region: Hudson Valley venison, Montauk lobster, herbs from the World Trade Center greenmarket, beef Wellington, and lunch specials and smaller dishes to bring in tourists alongside the executives. Kevin Zraly ran the wine programme from 1976; Veuve Clicquot Yellow Label was the house Champagne. About 450 people worked across the three rooms. In 2000 it reported $37 million in revenue, the highest-grossing restaurant in the United States. Ruth Reichl gave it two stars in The New York Times on December 31, 1997. THIS SAVE BEGINS IN JANUARY 1999: keep the story in its own time, among the people and events of the late 1990s, and do not foreshadow or depict later events. Money is in 1999 dollars. The dining-room appetizers and main courses, with their prices, are from a Lomonaco-era Windows on the World dinner menu (1997-2001, summer); the bar dishes are from the Greatest Bar on Earth's 1996 opening menu and beef Wellington from a later account of his Windows dishes; the desserts, cheeses and all other prices are stand-ins or estimates, and staff names, rent and the local events are invented; the history above is from published sources.

menu.identity: Michael Lomonaco's American cooking from Hudson Valley and Long Island farms in the dining room, an international menu from the chef stations in the Greatest Bar on Earth, and Kevin Zraly's wine list.

team.name: Anthony Ruggiero
team.bio: Executive chef's number two in the kitchen: runs a brigade of more than a hundred through lunch, dinner, the bar menu and a five-hundred-cover banquet on the same night.

team.name: Marisol Reyes
team.bio: Sous chef on the dining-room line; came up through the banquet kitchen on the 106th floor.

team.name: Henri Lacaze
team.bio: Pastry chef. The soufflés go out on the minute, and the wedding cakes go up in the freight elevator.

team.name: Paul Whitcombe
team.bio: Cellar master for one of the biggest wine lists in America, and a teacher at the wine school two nights a week.

team.name: Evelyn Park
team.bio: Director of the dining room. Seats the tourists by the window, the regulars where they like, and never lets a jacket-and-tie rule start an argument.

policies.name: Union health and welfare fund
policies.blurb: Most of the staff belong to the hotel and restaurant workers' union, and the contract pays into its health fund.

policies.name: Family meal before service
policies.blurb: Staff eat together in the employee dining room before lunch and dinner.
